name: Tai Thanh
catalog_citation: Ferlus, Michel. 2008. "The Tai dialects of Nghệ An, Vietnam (Tay Daeng, Tay Yo, Tay Muong)." In Anthony V. N. Diller, Jerold A. Edmondson & Yongxian Luo (eds.), The Tai-Kadai Languages, 298-315. London & New York: Routledge. Read in the author's updated French version, "Les dialectes tai du Nghệ An, Vietnam (Tay Daeng, Tay Yo, Tay Muong)", HAL halshs-01617791 (deposited 17 Oct 2017), 24 pp., CC BY-NC-SA.
catalog_locator: HAL author version halshs-01617791: §3 'Généralités phonétiques', p. 4 (PDF p. 5), first paragraph and the paragraph beginning 'Les trois dialectes ont développé'; §4.3 'Système tonal', p. 6 (PDF p. 7), first paragraph with Figure 2 'Tons du tay thanh (Con Cuông, Nghệ An)'. In the copy we hold:, 190-192 and 275-283. Identity sentence §2 p. 3 (line 114): 'Les Tay Daeng [dɛːŋᴬ¹] (écrit aussi Dèng) sont appelés Tay Thanh ou Man Thanh par les Vietnamiens.'
catalog_quote: La structure du mot de base dans les trois dialectes, tay daeng (tay thanh), tay yo et tay muong, est strictement monosyllabique: CV(C)/T, (C: consonne; V: voyelle; T: ton). ... Les trois dialectes ont développé un même système tonal de base à six tons. Le nombre des tons a pu ultérieurement se réduire à cinq, suite à des confusions qui peuvent varier selon les dialectes. ... Le tay thanh (tay daeng du Nghệ An) parlé à Con Cuông atteste un système tonal à cinq unités, les tons B2 et C1 s’étant confondus. D’après d’autres sources disponibles (Gedney 1964, Robert 1941, Fénart 1920) cette situation caractérise également les dialectes tay daeng parlés au Thanh Hóa et au Laos.
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

new_statements.quote: All the languages dealt with here (W B R S) have, in addition to the types of syllables already described, other syllables having weak stress, usually prefixed to a normal syllable. Such weak syllables usually have a short a vowel, though sometimes other vowels occur. The tone on such syllables tends to be neutralized to a mid level pitch in all four languages. [...] It is noteworthy that of the four languages here studied, Siamese has by far the greatest number of such weak syllables, Red Tai somewhat fewer, Black Tai still fewer, and in White Tai they are infrequent.
new_statements.citation: Gedney, William J. 1964. "A comparative sketch of White, Black and Red Tai." The Social Science Review (Bangkok), special number: 1-47; reprinted in R. J. Bickner, J. Hartmann, T. J. Hudak & P. Peyasantiwong (eds), Selected Papers on Comparative Tai Studies (Michigan Papers on South and Southeast Asia 29), Ann Arbor: University of Michigan, 1989, 415-462.
new_statements.locator: p. 421 of the 1989 reprint (PDF page 7), paragraph following the Red Tai checked-syllable tones; scanned text in lines 362-375
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: The quotation was checked again. Rendered PDF page 7 of (page number 421 printed at foot) and read the image: the quoted passage is there verbatim, including the elided middle sentence ('Though this phenomenon would have to be dealt with in a more thorough analysis of each language.. S măphraaw4 or mă4 phraaw4 "coconut."'). The scanned file (lines 362-375) drops the left-margin letter on several lines but the image is clean. The later 'unstressed position' remarks (the scanned text = reprint pp. 453-458) are as the first reader describes: attributions of tone/vowel irregularities in 'one', 'how many', the classifier to1, 'equal', 'not' to reduction in unstressed position. Gedney p. 418 also…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Red Tai (Tay Daeng, which Ferlus 2008 identifies with Tay Thanh/Man Thanh) is a tone language whose normal syllables each carry a distinctive tone; the only stress statement is that a minor prefixed syllable (usually short a) has weak stress and a neutralized mid-level tone, so in such words prominence lies on the final, full (toned) syllable. Ferlus 2008, the only description of Nghệ An Tay Thanh itself, states the word is strictly monosyllabic CV(C)/T and says nothing about stress.
new_statements.exceptions: Weak syllables 'usually have a short a vowel, though sometimes other vowels occur'; the phenomenon is described as infrequent in the basic vocabulary, and Gedney says it 'would have to be dealt with in a more thorough analysis of each language'. Later (pp. 454, 458-459) tone/vowel irregularities in some words (e.g. 'one', 'how many', classifier to1, 'not', 'equal') are attributed to reduction 'in unstressed position'.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level: monosyllabic words carry a full tone; sesquisyllabic words consist of a weak-stressed prefixed minor syllable plus a normal (toned) syllable. The remark is made for all four languages compared (White, Black, Red Tai, Siamese); the Red Tai data are from Ban Na Yon, Sam Neua province, Laos, elicited in Vientiane in 1964 ('only a few hours' of work, p. 418). No word-level stress rule beyond this is given; nothing on phrase stress.
new_statements.first_reading: tone language with a stress statement
new_statements.identity_note: Identity caveat, substantial. The quoted stress statement is Gedney's, about Red Tai (tay4 leeng1) of Ban Na Yon, Sam Neua province, Laos, which under ISO/Glottolog is Tai Daeng [tyr] = taid1249 (Tai Daeng-Meuay), not [tmm]. The link to tait1248 rests on Ferlus 2008 (the only description of the Nghệ An variety), who states that the Tay Daeng 'sont appelés Tay Thanh ou Man Thanh par les Vietnamiens', titles his section '4. Tay Daeng (ou Tay Thanh)', uses Gedney 1964 as one of its sources, and reports that the 5-tone system of Tay Thanh of Con Cuông (B2 = C1 merged) also characterises the Tay Daeng dialects of Thanh Hóa and Laos per Gedney 1964. Ferlus's own Tay Thanh description (Con Cuông, Nghệ An) is silent on stress (word 'strictement monosyllabique CV(C)/T'). Vietnamese usage: Tày Thanh = Man Thanh = Tay Nhài, Nghệ An and Thanh Hóa. If the catalog keys strictly by ISO code, file the Gedney statement under taid1249 and mark tait1248 as accessible description is silent on stress (Ferlus 2008).

sources.note: Silent on stress. Section 3 states the basic word in Tay Daeng (= Tay Thanh), Tay Yo and Tay Muong is 'strictement monosyllabique: CV(C)/T'; section 4.3 gives the 5-tone system of Tay Thanh of Con Cuong (B2 = C1 merged). Explicitly: 'Les Tay Daeng.. sont appelés Tay Thanh ou Man Thanh par les Vietnamiens' (p. 3) and cites Gedney 1964 as a source for its Tay Daeng data.
